title: A doctor is dismissing your symptoms
lede: Third appointment. You are tired, in pain, or frightened, and you have been told it is stress, or your age, or that the tests were normal so there is nothing wrong. You are being managed out of the room.

blocks.text: Third appointment. You are tired, in pain, or frightened, and you have been told it is stress, or your age, or that the tests were normal so there is nothing wrong. You are being managed out of the room.

items: Ten-minute appointments reward specific, structured information and punish narrative. How you present is unfairly but genuinely decisive.
"Tests normal" means those tests did not detect that condition. It is not the same as nothing being wrong, and saying so out loud is legitimate.
Certain phrases change clinical behaviour because they engage professional responsibility and the medical record. Using them is not rudeness.
Some groups are measurably more likely to be dismissed. If that is you, you need the structured approach more, not less.

items.detail: Onset date, frequency, duration, severity, triggers, what has changed. One page. Hand it over and ask for it to be added to your record.
"I have stopped driving," "I cannot lift my child," "I have missed nine days of work." Functional loss is heard where "tired" is not.

items.move: Ask for the differential out loud
items.detail: "What else could this be, and what would rule it out?" It shifts the encounter from reassurance to reasoning.

items.move: Ask for your concern to be recorded
items.detail: Requesting documentation of a declined test or an unaddressed concern changes the dynamic immediately and appropriately.
A second person in the room measurably changes how consultations go, and they remember what you will not.

items.move: Ask for a referral or second opinion explicitly
items.detail: Name it. Unnamed wishes do not get actioned.

items.say: "In three months I have gone from running twice a week to not managing the stairs without stopping. That is what I need explained."
"I understand the blood tests were normal. What else could cause this, and what would we do to rule those out?"
"I would like it noted that I raised this and that a scan was not felt necessary. Could you put that in my notes please?"
"I would like to be referred to a specialist. If you do not think that is appropriate, can you explain what would need to change for a referral to happen?"

items: Presenting eleven symptoms in random order. Prioritise the three that matter most.
Anger. It is completely understandable and it reliably gets you labelled in the notes, which follows you.
Arriving with a self-diagnosis and demanding confirmation. Bring evidence and questions instead.
Giving up after two appointments. Persistence with structure is what gets diagnoses.
Downplaying to be a good patient. "It is not that bad" is recorded exactly as you say it.
Request your records and read them. It is your right and it reveals what is actually being considered.
Keep a daily one-line symptom log. Longitudinal data is very hard for any clinician to dismiss.
Change practitioner if the relationship is not working. That is legitimate, not disloyal.
Use the formal patient advocacy or complaints route if you are being repeatedly refused. It produces written reasons.

limit: For red-flag symptoms — sudden severe headache, chest pain, one-sided weakness, slurred speech, unexplained weight loss, coughing blood, a new lump, or loss of vision — go to emergency care rather than waiting for another appointment.
